description: RoboBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as embodied brains for robotic manipulation. It defines five dimensions—instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis—spanning 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs. Data combines large-scale real-world robotic datasets with curated in-house collection, and includes a novel MLLM-as-world-simulator framework for evaluating long-horizon planning.
name: RoboBench
publisher: Peking University / Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A human study was conducted on 438 uniformly sampled long-horizon planning tasks to validate the evaluation metric. Expert annotators assigned holistic scores (0–20) referencing ground-truth planning lists. The MLLM-as-world-simulator method achieved a higher Pearson correlation coefficient with human judgments (r=0.83) compared to the LLM-based pairwise trajectory scoring baseline (r=0.73).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom in-house annotation pipeline with human expert annotators
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were created through a multi-stage pipeline: (1) preprocessing raw data; (2) annotation using VLMs, detection models, or human experts; (3) Q&A format generation. Gemini generated structured annotations (task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, metadata). Human annotators refined these annotations. A two-stage quality control process was applied: data filtering during construction (general and task-specific filters) and post-construction validation by 20 professionally trained annotators checking linguistic clarity, answerability, and correctness. A majority-vote strategy was also applied.
rai:dataBiases: The planning data primarily focuses on concrete action execution without explicitly distinguishing between left-right arm assignments or positional movements, which may bias cross-embodiment planning evaluation. Performance drops sharply when tasks involve uncommon objects, suggesting the data may be biased toward common, well-seen objects.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from open-source and in-house robotic datasets. For planning, a planning pool was built from high-quality robotic videos from multiple sources. Perception data was constructed across four aspects using real robot data, curated static attributes, GPT-generated properties, Gemini-segmented video steps, and human-labeled bounding boxes. Failure analysis data was collected from RoboMIND and labeled by experts, while planning-level failures were synthesized by perturbing correct instructions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data includes high-quality robotic videos from multiple open-source datasets (including RoboMIND, and others from Collaboration et al., Lin et al., Liu et al., Fang et al., Mu et al., Yang et al.), real robot data with type and view metadata, curated static object attributes, and in-house collected robotic manipulation data.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: Current MLLMs exhibit difficulties with implicit instruction comprehension, spatiotemporal reasoning, cross-scenario planning, fine-grained affordance understanding, and execution failure diagnosis. Planning-level failure data was synthesized due to lack of real-world planning failure data. The benchmark relies on an MLLM as world simulator for evaluation, which may introduce subjectivity.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Explicit instructions were rewritten into implicit (demand-based) forms using LLMs to create paired explicit-implicit instruction data. Planning-level failures were synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order). Representative frames were sampled from the planning pool for affordance annotation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data preprocessing included: extracting frame sequences from robotic videos as standardized inputs; applying general and task-specific filters (e.g., image quality checks, task validity, excluding single-arm data from dual-arm tasks); standardizing all data into multiple-choice QA format; mapping natural language steps into predefined function templates; and converting explicit instructions into implicit forms using LLMs.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as embodied brains for robotic manipulation; benchmarking high-level cognitive capabilities including instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis; guiding the development of next-generation MLLMs toward more robust robotic intelligence.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Gemini (used for video segmentation, generating structured annotations including task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, and metadata); GPT (used for generating functional object properties and distractors, and for rewriting explicit instructions into implicit forms); VLMs and detection models (used in the annotation pipeline for various sub-benchmarks)

evidence.name: We introduce RoboBench, a benchmark that systematically evaluates multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as embodied brains.
evidence.description: RoboBench defines five dimensions—instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis—spanning 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs. To ensure realism, we curate datasets across diverse embodiments, attribute-rich objects, multi-view scenes, and memory-driven navigation, drawing from large-scale real robotic data and in-house collection.

evidence.rai:dataCollection: To evaluate the five cognitive dimensions, we build datasets from open-source and in-house robotic data, enriched with MLLM- and human-provided annotations, aligning each sub-benchmark with the embodied task pipeline for realism.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We build datasets from open-source and in-house robotic data, enriched with MLLM- and human-provided annotations. We build a planning pool from high-quality robotic videos Collaboration et al. (2023); Lin et al. (2024a); Liu et al. (2024b;c); Fang et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2024); Mu et al. (2023); Yang et al. Execution-level failures (e.g., position misalignment, trajectory deviations, gripper errors) are collected from RoboMIND Wu et al. (2024) and labeled by experts.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We adopt a two-stage quality control process to ensure benchmark quality: data filtering during construction and post-construction validation. After data construction, we recruite 20 professionally trained annotators to conduct comprehensive quality inspections, validating linguistic clarity, answerability, and correctness. We further adopt a majority-vote strategy: items that all models solve correctly are removed, whereas items all models fail to solve undergo manual review and correction.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Each workflow generally follows three stages—preprocessing, annotation with VLMs, detection models or human experts, and Q&A format generation.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We apply both general and task-specific filters. General criteria address image quality and task validity, while sub-benchmarks have tailored rules—such as excluding single-arm data from dual-arm tasks.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Explicit instructions are drawn from daily-life scenarios with clearly specified actions and targets, whereas implicit instructions are obtained by rewriting them into demand-based requests using LLMs. Planning-level failures are synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order) due to lack of real-world planning failure data.

evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We uniformly sampled 438 long-horizon tasks from the Q1 planning inference sets, covering diverse dimensions and model outputs. Expert annotators (with prior training) assigned holistic scores in the range 0–20, referencing the ground-truth planning list. Our method achieve a higher Pearson correlation coefficient with human judgments, shown in Figure 6b and 6c, indicating stronger consistency and validating the effectiveness of the proposed metric.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: RoboBench provides a comprehensive scaffold to quantify high-level cognition, clarify the role of the embodied brain, and guide the development of next-generation MLLMs toward more robust robotic intelligence.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: RoboBench provides a comprehensive scaffold to quantify high-level cognition, clarify the role of the embodied brain, and guide the development of next-generation MLLMs toward more robust robotic intelligence. We conduct large-scale systematic evaluation of SOTA MLLMs, establishing a leaderboard and offering actionable insights for advancing the embodied brain in robotic AI.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: planning-level failures are synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order) due to lack of real-world planning failure data. Experiments on 14 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal fundamental limitations: difficulties with implicit instruction comprehension, spatiotemporal reasoning, cross-scenario planning, fine-grained affordance understanding, and execution failure diagnosis.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Current models often fail to coordinate dual-arm operations or perform mobile manipulation, resulting in suboptimal spatial search and movement decisions. We attribute this to the nature of existing planning data, which primarily focuses on concrete action execution without explicitly distinguishing between left–right arm assignments or positional movements. Performance drops sharply when tasks involve uncommon objects, symbolic reasoning, or world knowledge, suggesting weak integration of heterogeneous information. In contrast, results on common, well-seen objects remain relatively acceptable
